repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 1:1 as the book’s vision superscription because its regnal frame is complete before the direct summons begins at 1:2. The rejected 1:1-20 unit preserves context but loses a marked genre transition; the canonical objection survives only as a non-naked-presentation warning.

primary_reviews.support: The Hebrew superscription supplies subject, object, geographic scope, and regnal dating within verse 1; the address to heavens starts a different speech act in verse 2.

primary_reviews.support: Bibliographic framing closes before the opening cosmic audience is summoned, so heading and accusation perform distinguishable literary work.

primary_reviews.counterevidence: The verse is still an observable canonical form boundary and can remain a child when its parent is mandatory.

repairs.boss_rationale: End the first accusation at 1:9: the remnant comparison answers the desolation sequence, while 1:10 names a new audience and shifts from national ruin to rejected sacrifice. primary_reviews.support: The opening imperatives summon cosmic witnesses, and the remnant conditional at 1:9 gives the devastation catalogue a grammatical and rhetorical close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The lawsuit accusation continues conceptually into the cultic charges that follow.

primary_reviews.support: Rebellious-family, diseased-body, and besieged-city images form a descending sequence completed by the Sodom survival comparison.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 2-20 together can be heard as one broad prosecution and invitation.

primary_reviews.support: No internal cross-reference independently establishes 1:9 as a retrieval seam; the decision rests on the local address and image progression.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Keeping 1:2-9 inside the full 1:1-31 parent protects the larger lawsuit setting.

repairs.defensible_basis: “Hear” and “listen” addressed to Sodom and Gomorrah begin a new disputation about sacrifices, assemblies, prayer, cleansing, and willing obedience. The unit closes at 1:20 with the antithetical eat/be-eaten verdict and the mouth-of-YHWH formula; absorbing 1:2-9 would erase the vocative reset and its cultic focus.
repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 1:10-20 as the worship indictment and cleansing appeal, ending where the divine-mouth attestation seals its alternatives. primary_reviews.support: Paired hearing imperatives open the address, and the concluding ki pi YHWH dibber formula marks the stated choice as complete at verse 20.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Sodom language also echoes verse 9, binding this speech to the preceding devastation accusation.

primary_reviews.support: Rejected ritual, bloodstained hands, washing, justice, and the color reversal advance as one accusation-to-invitation arc.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The larger lawsuit begun at 1:2 remains the governing parent and should accompany isolated retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical reuse may illuminate individual lines, but it cannot choose between the local 1:10-20 child and the 1:2-20 macro-unit.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The explicit 1:10 address and 1:20 seal provide adequate local evidence without importing later usage.

repairs.defensible_basis: The exclamation “How has the faithful city become a prostitute?” opens a city lament whose corrupt silver, rulers, and injustice are answered by smelting, restored judges, and the final oak-and-garden fire at 1:31. repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 1:21-31 together because the lament’s city question receives its complete judicial and metallurgical answer before the unquenchable-fire ending. primary_reviews.support: The opening lament particle introduces the city’s reversal, while the adversative divine declaration at 1:24 answers rather than abandons that complaint.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 24 has a messenger-style declaration and could be treated as the start of a judgment response.

primary_reviews.support: Debased metal at the accusation is reversed by smelting in the answer, and the oak/garden combustion supplies the poem’s terminal image.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The response contains its own restoration and judgment movements that could be internal children.

primary_reviews.support: Separating 1:24-31 risks presenting purification without the city conditions named in 1:21-23; the integrated child retains the problem-solution relation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A user seeking the restoration oracle may prefer a hydrated 1:24-31 child.

repairs.defensible_basis: The phrase “the word that Isaiah son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem” is a localized prophetic heading complete at 2:1, before the latter-days poem begins. repairs.boss_rationale: Surface 2:1 as a heading because its formula identifies the message and its scope, whereas 2:2 begins with an eschatological time expression and poetic scene. primary_reviews.support: Hadavar asher hazah plus prophet and geographic object constitutes a nominal heading; the temporal vehayah be’acharit hayyamim starts at verse 2.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Masoretic presentation does not itself decide whether the heading should be a standalone retrieval result.

primary_reviews.support: Heading, nations poem, and house-of-Jacob exhortation can be read as a single 2:1-5 Zion movement before the causal turn at 2:6.

primary_reviews.support: Parallel prophetic wording elsewhere confirms the heading genre but does not settle whether it is returned independently.

repairs.boss_rationale: End the nations instruction poem at 2:4, where its movement from ascent to Torah to international judgment culminates in disarmament. primary_reviews.support: The sequence of plural nation speech and divine adjudication closes with paired negated war clauses; verse 5 begins a second-person plural summons.

primary_reviews.support: Verse 5 answers the nations’ “come, let us go up” language and can complete a 2:1-5 call-and-response pattern.

primary_reviews.support: A 2:2-4 result preserves the famous vision as a complete scene when the heading and neighboring exhortation are supplied by parent hydration.

repairs.defensible_basis: The house-of-Jacob command to walk in divine light at 2:5 becomes the standard against which abandonment, wealth, idols, and human pride are exposed. repairs.boss_rationale: Preserve 2:5-22 as the abasement oracle because verse 5 names its audience and ethical summons, while verse 22 closes with a final imperative about humanity. primary_reviews.support: Verse 5 is an imperative to Jacob, but the causal ki at 2:6 can attach what follows either as grounds for that command or as a distinct accusation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Repetition of being humbled and entering rocks still unifies 2:6-22 independently of verse 5.

primary_reviews.support: The exhortation in 2:5 echoes the ascent poem and may close 2:1-5, leaving the sustained day-and-pride indictment to start at 2:6.

primary_reviews.support: Beginning with “house of Jacob” prevents a detached judgment catalogue from appearing as an unaddressed universal abstraction.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Parent hydration already identifies the larger Zion-and-abasement cycle, so 2:6 can remain intelligible.

repairs.defensible_basis: The removal of every support in Jerusalem opens a leadership-collapse oracle that proceeds through social inversion and culminates in YHWH standing to judge elders and princes for crushing the poor at 3:15. repairs.boss_rationale: Close the leadership and courtroom movement at 3:15, after the accusation against those who grind the faces of the poor. The daughters-of-Zion speech beginning at 3:16 shares the city’s judgment setting but introduces a new addressee, imagery system, and consequence extending across the chapter boundary.

primary_reviews.support: Removal formulae and leadership nouns dominate 3:1-12; the courtroom stance and direct elder-prince accusation complete that concern in 3:13-15.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The messenger declaration in 3:16 remains within the same broad Jerusalem judgment discourse.

primary_reviews.support: The unit moves coherently from institutional deprivation to chaotic replacements and then to judicial accountability for failed governance.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A chapter-scale 3:1-4:1 composition would keep all social groups inside one collapse tableau.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieving through 3:15 preserves the causal link between leadership failure and harm to vulnerable people instead of isolating the courtroom charge.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The subsequent address supplies another concrete manifestation of the city’s pride and loss.

repairs.defensible_basis: A fresh declaration about the daughters of Zion begins at 3:16, catalogues ornament and its removal, reaches city desolation at 3:26, and continues naturally to seven women seeking one man in 4:1. repairs.boss_rationale: Use the cross-chapter 3:16-4:1 span because its female addressee, adornment reversal, male-loss lament, and seven-women outcome form one descending sequence. primary_reviews.support: The opening wayyo’mer plus daughters-of-Zion subject governs the punishment catalogue; 4:1 continues with feminine action before 4:2’s “in that day” renewal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 3:26 has a strong city-lament image that can sound like a poetic close.

primary_reviews.support: Adornment becomes shame, men fall, gates lament, and the scarcity scene in 4:1 supplies the social aftermath rather than a new episode.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift from plural daughters to seven women could be treated as a brief concluding child.

primary_reviews.support: Crossing the chapter protects the causal sequence and exposes a mechanical chapter split as the weaker retrieval boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit still needs the larger 3:1-4:6 parent to avoid detaching it from leadership judgment and later restoration.

repairs.defensible_basis: “In that day” at 4:2 reverses the preceding shame with branch, surviving remnant, cleansing, renewed cloud-and-fire, canopy, shade, and refuge, ending at 4:6. Attaching 4:1 would import the prior judgment’s final consequence; continuing into 5:1 would cross into an explicitly introduced vineyard song.
repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 4:2-6 as the purified-Zion restoration oracle because its remnant and cleansing movement resolves in a complete protective-canopy image. Both neighboring alternatives lose to marked form changes: 4:1 concludes scarcity, and 5:1 begins a first-person song for the beloved.

primary_reviews.support: Bayyom hahu opens the reversal, and creation/cloud/tabernacle language develops without a new speech formula through the refuge close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same temporal formula recurs frequently and cannot establish a seam by itself.

primary_reviews.support: Purification of survivors leads to protective presence over the assembly, giving the short restoration poem an internal beginning, transformation, and sheltering result.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its meaning is intentionally contrastive with 3:16-4:1 and should retain parent-level linkage.

primary_reviews.support: A separate child allows the restoration movement to be found without swallowing the preceding judgment, while parent hydration keeps their designed contrast visible.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Isolated retrieval may invite identity claims about the “branch” that local chunking cannot decide.

repairs.defensible_basis: The invitation to sing for the beloved introduces vineyard preparation, failed fruit, a judicial appeal, and threatened dismantling; 5:7 then identifies vineyard, plants, justice, and bloodshed in matching wordplay. Splitting before the interpretation leaves the song’s legal riddle unanswered, while 5:8 begins a new woe catalogue.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 5:1-7 intact as vineyard song plus juridical interpretation, ending where the expected justice/righteousness contrasts are decoded. An independent 5:1-6 poem is formally possible, but its withheld referents and courtroom question make verse 7 the necessary completion rather than an optional appendix.

primary_reviews.support: The first-person song shifts to direct vineyard address and then to the explanatory ki; the justice/bloodshed and righteousness/cry paronomasia seals the interpretation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 7 changes from figurative narrative to explicit prophetic application and can be marked internally.

primary_reviews.support: Love song, disappointed cultivation, audience verdict, destruction sentence, and riddle solution constitute one carefully staged forensic performance.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A reader studying poetic form may want the song proper distinguished from its interpretive gloss.

primary_reviews.support: Returning the metaphor without verse 7 would encourage uncontrolled identification; including the interpretation anchors the vineyard’s local function.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later vineyard reuse can illuminate reception but must not determine this seam.

repairs.defensible_basis: A chain of repeated “woe” accusations addresses land accumulation, drunken feasting, deliberate sin, moral inversion, self-wisdom, and corrupt justice, with matching consequences. The root-and-blossom fire image closes this governed catalogue at 5:24; atomizing each woe loses their cumulative prosecution, whereas 5:25 changes to the anger refrain and invasion horizon.
repairs.boss_rationale: Treat 5:8-24 as the woe catalogue because recurring accusation-and-verdict panels accumulate toward the rejected-instruction summary at its endpoint. Six smaller sayings remain useful internal movements, but none gains enough independence to outweigh the catalogue’s shared forensic function and final causal judgment.

primary_reviews.support: Repeated hoy openings mark coordinated strophes, and the final al-ken clause explains their destruction by rejection of divine instruction.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Each woe has a distinct addressee, image, and sanction and could be separately retrieved with siblings.

primary_reviews.support: The catalogue escalates from property and appetite to speech, moral categories, wisdom claims, and public justice before a consuming verdict.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A six-child representation would expose the patterned architecture more explicitly.

primary_reviews.support: The larger unit prevents one accusation from being detached from parallel charges and their common legal conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Search precision for a particular woe may require internal anchors without promoting them to top-level chunks.

repairs.defensible_basis: The therefore clause at 5:25 introduces divine anger, earthquake, corpses, and the first outstretched-hand refrain, then 5:26-30 expands the threat into a summoned distant army ending in sea-like darkness. Attaching verse 25 backward respects causation but leaves its refrain and invasion imagery separated from the coda they initiate.
repairs.boss_rationale: Place 5:25 forward with 5:26-30 because the anger refrain opens a new scale of judgment and the signal-to-nations sequence completes it at the darkness ending. The backward attachment to the sixth woe remains plausible grammatical dissent, but the frozen boundary better preserves the invasion tableau as a whole.

primary_reviews.support: The al-ken at 5:25 points backward to rejected instruction in 5:24, and the anger refrain can function as the preceding woe catalogue’s sentence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same verse introduces the recurring outstretched-hand formula and landscape of national attack developed through verse 30.

primary_reviews.support: Earthquake devastation broadens into the banner, swift invaders, roaring, and darkened land, producing one cinematic coda after the local woes.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 25 has retrospective logic and could serve as a hinge shared by both movements.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieval beginning at 5:25 may hide the therefore relation to the catalogue’s final rejection-of-instruction verdict.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Hydrating 5:25-30 with the full chapter retains that cause while keeping the invasion sequence undivided.

challenge.claim: The frozen child starts with a backward-pointing conclusion that may appear causeless.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require chapter-parent hydration and retain 5:25-backward attachment as an append-only boundary appeal.

repairs.defensible_basis: The death-year date opens a throne vision whose holiness acclamation, smoke, confession, coal purification, commission dialogue, hardening instruction, how-long question, devastation, and stump image run through 6:13. Splits at 6:8 or 6:9 sever preparation from the commission it enables or command from its requested duration.
repairs.boss_rationale: Preserve all of chapter 6 as the dated throne-vision commission: every stage advances one scene, and the stump coda answers the prophet’s duration question. Smaller vision, purification, and commissioning movements are real internal parts, but the continuous speaker exchange gives no better surfaced endpoint before 6:13.

primary_reviews.support: Narrative wayyiqtol sequencing, direct speech, and the prophet’s reply remain continuous from the throne sight through the final seed metaphor.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The whom-shall-I-send question at 6:8 and imperative at 6:9 are strong internal discourse turns.

primary_reviews.support: Vision, unworthiness, cleansing, volunteering, commission, protest, and answer form a single call narrative with no unresolved action.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Independent retrieval of 6:1-8 or 6:9-13 could serve form-specific study if compulsory siblings accompany it.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the scene whole guards against quoting either the holiness acclamation or hardening commission without the narrative response around it.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A whole-chapter unit may receive a mechanical confidence penalty despite strong literary evidence.

repairs.defensible_basis: A dated coalition crisis brings Ahaz, Isaiah, and the named child to the aqueduct, followed by the command not to fear, the enemies’ plan, and the faith warning at 7:9. Extending through 7:17 merges this first reassurance with a renewed divine speech and Ahaz’s separate refusal-and-sign dialogue beginning in 7:10.
repairs.boss_rationale: End the initial crisis encounter at the faith warning in 7:9 because its narrative setup and first oracle are complete before YHWH spoke again reopens the exchange. The 7:1-17 parent is valuable for hydration, but it masks two distinct speech rounds and their different rhetorical functions.

primary_reviews.support: Dating and movement to the conduit establish the scene; the paired im-lo ta’aminu and lo te’amenu wordplay gives the first speech a terminal warning.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same encounter and addressee continue after verse 9, so the seam is a speech-round boundary rather than a scene change.

primary_reviews.support: Fear report, symbolic child, reassurance, adversary plan, counter-oracle, and faith condition complete the first dramatic exchange.

repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 7:10-17 as the royal sign dialogue and oracle, closing when the promised time scale reaches the announced political reversal. The famous central verse is not its own literary unit, and the repeated temporal panels after verse 17 are a new sequence despite thematic continuity.

primary_reviews.support: The dialogue boundaries are clear, but lexical and translation disputes within the sign wording cannot be settled from the correlated OSHB and UXLC witnesses alone.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Those unresolved semantic questions do not erase the renewed-speech opening or the 7:17 endpoint.

primary_reviews.support: The full dialogue prevents a celebrated sign line from being detached from speaker, audience, refusal, and temporal framing.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later canonical reuse is important context but neither identifies the child nor authorizes a preferred translation here.

repairs.boss_rationale: Surface 7:18-25 as the land-devastation cycle because its four temporal panels share Assyrian aftermath imagery and reach a complete agricultural desolation close. primary_reviews.support: Bayyom hahu recurs at verses 18, 20, 21, and 23, coordinating separate images under one temporal judgment frame.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Formula recurrence marks internal strophes and could support finer children rather than only the parent.

primary_reviews.support: Foreign swarm, razor, reduced herd, curds and honey, and abandoned vineyards progressively transform the land into a thorny wasteland.

repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 8:1-4 as the symbolic writing-and-naming sign because every commanded element receives narrative execution and interpretation by its endpoint. The Shiloah oracle shares the crisis but opens with a new speech formula and changes the governing image from child timing to floodwaters.

primary_reviews.support: Imperatives for tablet and stylus are followed by witness-taking, conception, naming, and the ki beterem timing explanation.

primary_reviews.support: Commission, authentication, performance, and near-term consequence provide the full grammar of a prophetic sign report.

primary_reviews.support: The complete action prevents the unusual name from being returned without the tablet, witnesses, and explicit timing function.

primary_reviews.support: The full span keeps the Immanuel refrain attached to both the threatened land and failed international counsel without deciding the name’s identity.

repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 9:8-10:4 as one four-strophe anger-refrain cycle because recurring closure, escalating social collapse, and the final corrupt-decree indictment share a single architecture. primary_reviews.support: The same refrain closes the panels at 9:12, 9:17, 9:21, and 10:4, overriding the intervening chapter coordinate.

repairs.defensible_basis: The woe to Assyria names the rod of anger, contrasts the instrument’s commission with its arrogant intent, answers boastful conquests through an axe-and-saw disputation, and ends with forest remnant imagery at 10:19. primary_reviews.support: Hoy opens direct address; interrogatives about axe, saw, rod, and staff govern the dispute until remnant-tree counting completes the judgment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Forest-felling imagery recurs at 10:33-34, linking this unit compositionally to the chapter’s close.

primary_reviews.support: Commissioned instrument becomes boastful conqueror, is rhetorically corrected, and is reduced from mighty forest to countable trees.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A 10:5-34 macro-oracle would preserve the full arrogance, remnant, march, and felling design.

primary_reviews.support: The selected child keeps the woe’s moral logic and verdict together without assigning historical or theological identity beyond the text.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Hydration with 10:5-34 is necessary to show how its forest image returns after the remnant interlude.

repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 10:20-27 as the remnant reassurance oracle, closing on the broken burden and yoke. primary_reviews.support: Bayyom hahu and repeated she’ar/remnant vocabulary open the promise, while burden and yoke language frames its terminal release.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The yoke-breaking expectation anticipates the invader’s final felling and may belong to a larger resolution sequence.

primary_reviews.support: Dependence reversal, remnant return, numbered judgment, Zion reassurance, and lifted burden create a coherent consolatory pause.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit’s deliverance is not dramatized until the march and forest collapse that follow.

primary_reviews.support: The span preserves both remnant limitation and reassurance, reducing the risk of retrieving promise without its severe judgment context.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Parent hydration should retain 10:5-34 so the attacker and outcome remain explicit.

repairs.defensible_basis: A rapid procession through Aiath, Migron, Michmash, the pass, Geba, Ramah, Gibeah, Gallim, Laishah, Anathoth, Madmenah, and Gebim stages the invader’s approach, before hand-shaking at Zion and divine lopping of the forest conclude at 10:34. repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 10:28-34 as the invasion-march and forest-felling tableau: the catalogue is not miscellaneous geography but a route whose suspense ends in sudden arboreal defeat. primary_reviews.support: Clipped travel verbs and place names generate pace until the hinneh divine-agent turn introduces branch lopping and Lebanon’s fall.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The final forest imagery echoes 10:17-19 and links distant parts of the Assyria oracle.

primary_reviews.support: Geographic proximity increases line by line, reaches a threatening gesture toward Zion, and reverses instantly in the felling coda.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Individual place notices have little independent literary closure and rely on the sequence as a whole.

primary_reviews.support: Treating the list as functional narrative avoids arbitrary micro-chunks based on proper names or modern geographic interest.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The scene needs the 10:5-34 parent to identify the force being judged and the earlier rod imagery.

repairs.boss_rationale: End the shoot-ruler and peaceable-creation poem at 11:9, where the harm prohibition and knowledge simile resolve its vision. Verse 10 lexically echoes the root, but changes to an in-that-day signal for peoples and then a second gathering; the frozen split respects that functional reset.

primary_reviews.support: The opening shoot and branch nouns govern the ruler description; the lo-yare’u prohibition plus earth-filled knowledge statement closes the created-order tableau.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Shoresh at 11:10 deliberately recalls the root image and may be the poem’s international culmination.

primary_reviews.support: Verse 10 can complete the movement from local ruler and holy mountain to the nations seeking the same root figure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its temporal formula, peoples subject, banner function, and rest/glory result open the remnant-gathering oracle that continues in verse 11.

repairs.defensible_basis: The in-that-day nations-root signal at 11:10 leads directly to another in-that-day act of recovering a remnant, raising a banner, resolving sibling hostility, subduing opposition, dividing the sea channel, and creating a highway at 11:16. repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 11:10-16 as the nations, remnant, and second-exodus oracle because verse 10 supplies its international signal and verse 16 closes with the explicit Assyria-to-Israel highway comparison. primary_reviews.support: Root language at 11:10 can close the preceding shoot poem before the second divine recovery begins at verse 11.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Banner, nations, dispersed people, and gathered remnant develop continuously from verse 10 through the highway ending.

challenge.claim: Verse 10 is a syntactic and lexical hinge with credible backward ownership.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Preserve 11:1-10 and 11:11-16 as the strongest rival segmentation for external adjudication.

primary_reviews.support: Nations seeking, remnant recovery, banner gathering, reconciled tribes, transformed waters, and highway compose one widening return tableau.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The return action proper begins only with the second in-that-day formula in verse 11.

primary_reviews.support: Forward attachment keeps the internationally visible root and banner with the dispersed-people retrieval context rather than exposing verse 10 alone.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The 11:1-16 parent is mandatory because both child routes depend on the root connection across the seam.

repairs.defensible_basis: Two in-that-day saying movements share thanksgiving after anger, trust, salvation imagery, water drawn with joy, proclamation among peoples, and a final Zion shout because the Holy One is present. Splitting 12:1-2 from 12:3-6 highlights singular and plural voices but weakens their answer-and-expansion relation before the Babylon burden begins.
repairs.boss_rationale: Preserve 12:1-6 as a thanksgiving and Zion-praise diptych: the singular confession supplies the salvation vocabulary that communal imperatives then widen toward public praise. The internal voice shift is real enough for stanza tagging, but both halves converge on one chapter-closing response to the preceding deliverance cycle.

primary_reviews.support: Ve’amarta bayyom hahu at verse 1 and a second saying formula at verse 4 coordinate parallel praise movements rather than unrelated poems.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Singular address in verses 1-2 and plural imperatives in 3-6 give each half its own voice and closure.

primary_reviews.support: A personal thanksgiving ending in song at verse 2 and a communal water-and-proclamation hymn beginning in verse 3 can surface as two complete children.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Shared salvation lexicon and the paired day formula make the two movements deliberately complementary.

challenge.claim: The whole-chapter parent may hide a genuine shift from individual confession to communal praise.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Allow 12:1-2 and 12:3-6 as internal hydrated children while retaining 12:1-6 as the surfaced unit.

primary_reviews.support: The diptych prevents water-drawing praise from being detached from the preceding statement that names salvation as its source.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Fine-grained search could benefit from child anchors if they cannot be mistaken for independent top-level units.

repairs.defensible_basis: The Babylon burden heading opens a summoned-army and day-of-YHWH desolation oracle, moves from cosmic terror to Babylon’s overthrow and deserted-city imagery, then reaches the Jacob-restoration and captor-reversal coda at 14:2. Ending at 13:22 drops the restoration answer; attaching 14:1-2 to the taunt places promise before its explicit taking-up formula.
repairs.boss_rationale: Use 13:1-14:2 as the Babylon burden with restoration coda because the desolated city receives its counter-movement in chosen Jacob, return, and reversed captivity. The chapter seam is mechanical, while the taunt does not formally begin until 14:3; nevertheless the two hinge verses remain a recorded attachment dispute.

primary_reviews.support: Massa Babylon supplies the oracle heading, and the ki compassion clause at 14:1 explains why devastation is followed by restoration before a new speech formula.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The compassion verses may provide the narrative setup for the taunt’s future rest from bondage.

primary_reviews.support: Babylon’s deserted-city close at 13:22 is strong, while 14:1-2 can introduce the reversal that makes the taunt possible.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The taunt’s explicit opening occurs at 14:3, and 14:1-2 answer the burden’s judgment with Jacob’s restoration.

challenge.claim: The frozen route assigns the two-verse restoration hinge backward despite its forward narrative function.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Preserve 13:1-22 plus 14:1-23 as the principal literary alternative for later review.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieving the taunt from 14:3 can hide the rest-from-sorrow setting supplied in 14:1-2.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Parent hydration across 13:1-14:23 can restore that setting without moving the active seam.

challenge.claim: The taunt child depends operationally on the restoration preface omitted by its start.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require shared-parent hydration and keep the 14:1-2 attachment open as nonblocking dissent.

repairs.defensible_basis: The explicit command that Israel take up a mashal opens at 14:3, addresses the oppressor through earth-rest, cypress and cedar response, underworld reception, fallen-height boast, grave disgrace, and dynastic erasure, ending with Babylon swept and emptied at 14:23. Including 14:1-2 would precede the formal taunt cue and dilute its voiced performance.
repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 14:3-23 as the royal taunt and destruction oracle because the mashal introduction governs every reversal through the final sweeping verdict. The previous restoration verses motivate the song but are not spoken within it; parent hydration preserves that relation without expanding the active form backward.

primary_reviews.support: Venasa’ta hammashal marks the formal speech start; direct address and underworld response continue until the divine extermination declaration closes at verse 23.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 3’s rest-from-oppression setting depends on the restoration material immediately before it.

primary_reviews.support: Mocking song, cosmic boast, descent, corpse humiliation, family judgment, and Babylon’s erasure form a sustained reversal performance.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Several internal voices and scenes could support stanza-level children under the taunt parent.

primary_reviews.support: Starting at the mashal formula constrains retrieval to the local taunt form and avoids importing later identity traditions as chunking evidence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The result still needs 13:1-14:23 hydration so speaker, target, and restoration context remain visible.

repairs.defensible_basis: A divine oath at 14:24 opens a compact Assyria oracle: purpose, breaking in the land, removed yoke, worldwide counsel, stretched hand, and unanswerable conclusion all finish at 14:27. Merging backward would cross the Babylon erasure verdict; extending forward would absorb a separately dated Philistia burden.
repairs.boss_rationale: Surface 14:24-27 as the sworn Assyria oracle because oath and rhetorical questions enclose one concise declaration of purpose. Its brevity is not fragmentation: both neighboring blocks identify different targets and possess their own formal openings, giving this unit clean independent boundaries.

primary_reviews.support: Nishba YHWH opens the sworn speech, and paired who-can-nullify/who-can-turn-it-back questions provide an unmistakable final cadence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The Assyria theme resumes material from 10:5-34, so anthology placement rather than narrative continuity governs context.

primary_reviews.support: Oath, announced act, burden release, universalized purpose, and challenge to reversal form a complete miniature oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A larger nations-oracle parent is necessary to explain its position between Babylon and Philistia blocks.

primary_reviews.support: The exact target and closure make this short child safer than joining it to a neighboring burden merely for size.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-reference to earlier Assyria material may aid interpretation but cannot relocate the seam.

repairs.defensible_basis: The death-year date and burden formula at 14:28 introduce a Philistia warning against rejoicing, followed by serpent succession, firstborn feeding, famine, smoke from the north, and a concluding answer about Zion’s foundation at 14:32. Joining 14:24-27 would combine differently targeted oracles and erase the fresh date.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 14:28-32 as the dated Philistia burden, ending with the envoy-answer question and Zion response. The Assyria oath before it may inform the geopolitical setting, but a new chronology, addressee, animal image, and messenger close establish a separate complete form.

primary_reviews.support: Bishnat mot plus hayah hammasa supplies a formal date-and-burden heading, while mah-ya’ane mal’akhe-goy closes with a direct answer.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The broken-rod image probably alludes to the preceding Assyria subject and creates deliberate adjacency.

primary_reviews.support: False celebration, escalating serpent imagery, social reversal, northern threat, and diplomatic answer complete the Philistia warning.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The oracle is compact enough that some systems may merge it into the surrounding chapter parent for retrieval simplicity.

primary_reviews.support: A separate dated burden prevents the target from being confused with Babylon or Assyria and preserves the final Zion answer with its question.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The identity of the rod or serpent must remain outside candidate boundary adjudication.

repairs.defensible_basis: The Moab burden sustains ruined-city cries, ascent and shaving lament, flight, waters, refugees, tribute appeal, proposed throne shelter, pride accusation, vineyard grief, failed sanctuary prayer, and an explicit former-word-now-three-years epilogue ending at 16:14. repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 15:1-16:14 as the Moab lament burden with timed epilogue because target, grief register, flight, appeal, pride, failed worship, and deadline remain one governed dossier. The 15:1-16:5, 16:6-12, and 16:13-14 divisions are defensible internal forms, preserved as dissent but not promoted here.

primary_reviews.support: The Moab burden heading governs repeated place names and lament verbs; zeh haddavar and ve’atta dibber at 16:13-14 explicitly label the deadline as a later speech about that same oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The former-word/now contrast makes 16:13-14 a distinct editorial or prophetic postscript with strong independent form.

primary_reviews.support: Lament-and-appeal through 16:5, pride-and-vineyard grief in 16:6-12, and the timed epilogue at 16:13-14 each possess recognizable local contours.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The latter movements answer the refugee appeal and remain explicitly about Moab under one burden heading.

challenge.claim: The active parent may be too coarse for three internally complete rhetorical movements.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Test three hydrated children while preserving 15:1-16:14 as their mandatory oracle parent.

primary_reviews.support: The larger span prevents the throne appeal, pride indictment, or three-year deadline from appearing without the Moab lament that gives each function.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A two-chapter result is costly for focused retrieval unless internal anchors and parent-sibling navigation are available.

repairs.defensible_basis: The Damascus burden opens with ruined-city and diminished-Jacob judgments, turns through gleaning and in-that-day regard for the Maker, contrasts abandoned strong cities, and ends with failed pleasant plantings and incurable grief at 17:11. The nations woe after it shares threat language but introduces its own exclamation, soundscape, rebuke, and evening-to-morning temporal miniature.

primary_reviews.support: Massa Dammeseq sets the target; gleaning, Maker-altars contrast, and the harvest-day result proceed without a new heading through verse 11.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 12-14 may broaden the same adversarial horizon from named cities to unnamed peoples.

primary_reviews.support: Loss moves from city to glory to harvest to cultic memory to doomed garden, providing a completed chain of diminishment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The in-that-day panels at 17:4 and 17:7 are strong internal turns that could be indexed below the parent.

primary_reviews.support: Ending at failed harvest keeps the named burden distinct from the generic nations woe and avoids target confusion in retrieval.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The Damascus and Jacob association remains interpretive context, not permission to harmonize historical sequences.

repairs.defensible_basis: A new woe at 17:12 compares tumultuous peoples to seas and mighty waters, then divine rebuke sends them like chaff and tumbleweed; evening terror becomes morning absence at 17:14. Retaining the whole chapter would bury this self-contained sound-and-time reversal beneath the preceding Damascus burden.
repairs.boss_rationale: Surface 17:12-14 as the roaring-nations coda because the woe cry, water similes, rebuke, flight, and overnight disappearance create a compact closed oracle. Its relation to chapter 18 or earlier invasion themes may inform context, but neither supplies a stronger boundary than the 17:12 opening and 17:14 morning close.

primary_reviews.support: Hoy opens plural tumult, repeated hamon/sha’on sound words build intensity, and the evening/morning antithesis gives the unit a crisp closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The final “portion of those who plunder us” can sound like a generalized coda to preceding national judgments.

primary_reviews.support: Roar, rebuke, dispersal, dusk fear, and dawn absence form a complete miniature dominated by auditory and temporal reversal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its brevity and generic target make it dependent on surrounding nation-oracle context.

primary_reviews.support: The narrow child is justified by form rather than fame, provided the 17:1-18:7 neighborhood remains available for orientation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical analogies to sea-tumult should not be allowed to name the nations or move the seam.

repairs.defensible_basis: The woe to the land of winged boats opens with envoys and a call for all inhabitants to watch the raised banner, pauses for a divine harvest observation, then depicts pruning before ripeness and ends with tribute brought to Zion at 18:7. repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 18:1-7 as the Cush envoy-harvest oracle because distant mission, universal signal, quiet divine observation, pre-harvest cutting, abandoned carcasses, and tribute arrive in one arc. primary_reviews.support: Hoy identifies the distant land; imperative messenger speech yields to ki koh amar YHWH, and ba’et hahi returns to the described people for the closing gift.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The messenger commission and divine harvest saying have different speakers and could be marked as component speeches.

primary_reviews.support: Dispatch, global visibility, waiting, ripening, pruning, exposure, and eventual tribute turn diplomatic imagery into a complete prophetic tableau.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The exact relation between the envoys and harvest remains implicit, which weakens fine-grained causal claims.

primary_reviews.support: Whole-chapter retrieval keeps the difficult images together and discourages assigning the distant people a settled identity from isolated lines.

repairs.defensible_basis: The Egypt burden begins with divine arrival, civic conflict, emptied spirit, failed counsel, harsh rule, Nile collapse, ruined industries, foolish princes, and staggering leadership, ending at 19:15 with no work for head or tail. primary_reviews.support: Massa Mitsrayim opens the burden; counsel and wisdom vocabulary dominates its center, and the head-tail/palm-reed merism closes the collapse comprehensively.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The chapter’s later transformation presupposes this judgment and could be retained in one judgment-to-blessing parent.

primary_reviews.support: Divine arrival cascades through society, river economy, crafts, court wisdom, and national agency until every status level is immobilized.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The environmental and failed-counsel sections are internally distinct enough for subordinate anchors.

primary_reviews.support: Separating at verse 15 prevents the judgment catalogue from swallowing the surprising worship-and-blessing reversals that deserve their own governed child.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Both units need the 19:1-25 parent so judgment and transformation are not presented as contradictory isolated predictions.

repairs.defensible_basis: Six coordinated in-that-day panels move Egypt from trembling fear to Judah-awareness, five oath-speaking cities, an altar and pillar, cry-and-deliverance, reciprocal knowing and healing, a highway with Assyria, and finally a three-nation blessing at 19:25. Atomizing each formula would hide the cumulative transformation from terror to shared blessing.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 19:16-25 as the in-that-day transformation cycle because repeated temporal openings stage successive changes whose climax blesses Egypt, Assyria, and Israel together. The panels are individually indexable, but their ordered expansion—not any one refrain alone—provides the unit’s completed rhetorical action.

primary_reviews.support: Bayyom hahu marks the panels at verses 16, 18, 19, 23, and 24, while blessing language at verse 25 supplies the cycle’s final divine speech.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Formula repetition also creates several clean internal seams rather than proving only a single large unit.

primary_reviews.support: Fear becomes speech, worship, answered distress, mutual knowledge, healed relations, open travel, and a triadic blessing in deliberate escalation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The altar-pillar and highway panels have enough independent imagery to be hydrated children.

primary_reviews.support: The complete sequence reduces the risk of extracting one nation or blessing line from the chapter’s progressive reconciliation movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No boundary claim may use later canonical theology to decide the identities or status of the three named peoples.

repairs.defensible_basis: The commander’s arrival at Ashdod dates a prose sign scene in which YHWH orders Isaiah to remove sackcloth and sandals, the prophet complies, and the three-year action is interpreted concerning Egypt and Cush before coastland observers voice dismay at 20:6. repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 20:1-6 as the dated prophetic sign-action narrative because its opening synchronism, command, execution, duration, interpretation, and concluding coastland question complete one scene. The prior Egypt oracle and following wilderness-sea burden differ in form even where their geopolitical vocabulary overlaps.

primary_reviews.support: A historical time clause opens narrative sequencing; commanded halok and performed ken asah are answered by the ka’asher interpretation before the audience’s concluding speech.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The sign’s referents and political setting connect tightly to the surrounding nation-oracle collection.

primary_reviews.support: Date, commission, bodily performance, symbolic duration, named interpretation, and witness reaction follow the standard shape of a complete sign report.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 1’s imperial event may be introductory context rather than part of the performed action proper.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the explanation and coastland response with the action prevents the prophet’s conduct from being retrieved as an unexplained anecdote.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Historical cross-references may inform context but cannot settle chronology or source dependence within this candidate task.

repairs.defensible_basis: The wilderness-of-the-sea burden opens a harsh vision, records anguish and disrupted banquet, then receives a watchman command at 21:6 whose report of riders culminates in “Babylon is fallen” and an address to the threshed people at 21:10. Splitting at verse 6 separates the distressing vision from the commissioned observation that interprets it.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 21:1-10 as the wilderness-sea vision and watchman report because burden, bodily response, surveillance, reported sight, fall announcement, and threshing address answer one another. A 1-5/6-10 division identifies a genuine scene turn, but neither half is as complete independently as the combined vision-report form.

primary_reviews.support: Massa opens the vision; ki koh amar at verse 6 commissions the lookout, whose shouted report and heard-from-YHWH attestation close the oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The command to station a watchman supplies a strong new speech and action boundary within the burden.

primary_reviews.support: Approaching storm, seer anguish, interrupted feast, patient lookout, rider report, city fall, and audience interpretation make one suspense-and-disclosure sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 1-5 and 6-10 could function as vision and interpretation children under mandatory parent hydration.

primary_reviews.support: The explicit watchman commission at 21:6 creates a retrievable report with its own task, observation, and announcement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Without 21:1-5, the report loses the burden heading and embodied prophetic reaction that frames its urgency.

challenge.claim: The frozen parent may be too broad for a complete 21:6-10 watchman-report child.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain 21:1-5 and 21:6-10 as a hydrated-child alternative without changing the current parent route.

repairs.defensible_basis: The Dumah burden consists of a repeated question from Seir—watchman, what of the night?—and the watchman’s dawn-yet-night answer with an invitation to inquire and return, ending at 21:12. repairs.boss_rationale: Surface 21:11-12 as the Dumah watchman dialogue: address, doubled nocturnal question, paradoxical response, and invitation form a complete two-verse exchange. primary_reviews.support: Massa Dumah identifies the unit, and direct qore elay plus repeated mah-millaylah lead to the watchman’s bounded answer and return imperative.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The enigmatic answer lacks narrative resolution and remains dependent on the nation-oracle setting.

primary_reviews.counterevidence: A short exchange can be over-emphasized if surfaced without the neighboring watchman and Arabia materials.

primary_reviews.support: The distinct burden title and complete speech exchange justify retrieval when the 21:1-17 parent is also supplied.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No interpretive tradition about Dumah or Seir is available locally to authorize identity claims.

repairs.defensible_basis: The Arabia burden opens with caravans lodging in the thickets, calls Tema to bring water and bread to fugitives, explains flight from warfare, and then gives a hired-worker-like one-year deadline for Kedar’s glory and archers to diminish at 21:17. Splitting at 21:16 detaches the timed verdict from the refugee conditions it answers.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 21:13-17 as the Arabia burden with timed Kedar coda because desert lodging, aid, flight, weapons, deadline, and remnant are one compact crisis oracle. Verse 16’s new divine-speech formula sharpens the forecast but does not supersede the burden’s target or create an independent scene.

primary_reviews.support: Massa ba’arav governs the caravan and Tema imperatives; ki koh amar at verse 16 supplies a temporal interpretation closed by the YHWH-spoke attestation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The one-year speech is formally distinct and could be indexed as a postscript similar to other timed codas.

primary_reviews.support: Displaced travelers, emergency hospitality, reason for flight, and quantified collapse develop a single desert-refuge scenario to conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Tema caravans and Kedar warriors are different named groups whose relationship is implied rather than narrated.

primary_reviews.support: Including both aid and deadline keeps humanitarian action beside the war pressure and prevents the forecast from appearing contextless.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The burden remains candidate evidence; historical identification and chronology require sources beyond this local pass.

repairs.defensible_basis: The valley-of-vision burden asks why the city has gone to the housetops, laments leaders captured without battle, surveys Elam-Kir assault and breached defenses, and indicts defensive preparations, feasting, and refusal to regard the Maker. The unforgiven-until-death oath closes at 22:14; adding 22:15 would introduce a newly named official and direct commission.
repairs.boss_rationale: End the valley vision at 22:14 because lament, siege observation, civic response, and revelry indictment culminate in a sworn verdict. The steward oracle following it occupies the same political world but has a fresh addressee and messenger instruction, so it should not be merged merely to fill the chapter.

primary_reviews.support: Massa ge-hizzayon opens the address, interrogatives and first-person lament govern its movement, and the revealed oath at verse 14 supplies a formal terminus.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Both this unit and the steward speech concern Jerusalem’s failed leadership and share the chapter setting.

primary_reviews.support: Confused celebration, unseen death, prophetic grief, approaching forces, human fortification, and fatal feasting form a complete city indictment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The survey of defenses at 22:8-11 and revelry at 12-14 are distinct internal accusation panels.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the revelry verdict within the burden prevents it from being detached as a generic saying about eating and drinking.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Historical reconstruction may aid context but cannot be treated as local boundary authority.

repairs.defensible_basis: A messenger command sends the prophet to the steward Shebna, challenges his tomb, announces removal, then shifts at 22:20 to Eliakim’s installation, key, stable peg, household weight, and a collapsing-peg coda at 22:25. Splitting those phases exposes real internal turns but risks separating deposition, replacement, elevation, and warning within one office-transfer oracle.
repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 22:15-25 as the steward deposition-and-installation oracle because the named office and transfer of authority bind its two addressees, while the final peg failure qualifies the installation imagery. The 15-19, 20-24, and 25 children remain serious alternatives, especially if the coda’s attachment receives independent review.

primary_reviews.support: A new messenger formula opens at verse 15 and a second in-that-day appointment begins at verse 20, but the final peg saying’s precise antecedent is disputed.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Stewardship, robe, sash, key, peg, and household load connect the removal and replacement movements lexically and institutionally.

primary_reviews.support: Self-made monument, humiliating removal, named successor, transferred insignia, secured authority, accumulated dependents, and collapse make a full reversal sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 20 is a conspicuous new temporal and personal start, while verse 25 can be heard as a separate corrective coda.

primary_reviews.support: Users may need to distinguish the Shebna judgment, Eliakim appointment, and peg-collapse saying rather than receive one composite official oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Separating them can imply independent referents or outcomes that the shared office-transfer parent is designed to constrain.

challenge.claim: The frozen parent may merge three address or image phases whose retrieval questions differ.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Review 22:15-19, 22:20-24, and 22:25 as mandatory-hydration children, preserving uncertainty about the coda’s referent.

repairs.defensible_basis: The Tyre burden opens with ships commanded to wail, cycles through coastland, Sidon, Egypt, sea, merchants, divine purpose against pride, and Assyrian ruin, then returns at 23:14 to the opening ship lament. Absorbing 23:15-18 would cross an explicit seventy-year temporal reset and a song-and-profit coda.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 23:1-14 as the principal Tyre lament and divine-purpose oracle because the renewed wail to ships forms an inclusion around its trade-city downfall. The later seventy-year forecast presupposes this loss but changes temporal horizon and rhetorical form, warranting a separate coda child.

primary_reviews.support: Massa Tsor and the ship-wail imperative begin the burden; the same imperative returns at verse 14 after the divine-purpose and Assyria explanations.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Target and commercial vocabulary continue in verses 15-18, so the coda remains part of the broader Tyre oracle.

primary_reviews.support: Maritime messengers, silenced port, international grief, merchant pride, divine overthrow, and renewed ship lament complete the main elegiac circuit.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal voices and geographic shifts make the lament composite even though its refrain unifies it.

primary_reviews.support: The inclusion gives a stronger endpoint than the chapter boundary and keeps trade imagery with the stated anti-pride purpose.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Economic and historical applications lie beyond the boundary task and should not inflate confidence.

repairs.defensible_basis: An explicit seventy-year transition at 23:15 introduces Tyre’s forgotten interval, a prostitute-song instruction, return to commerce, and the final redirection of profit as dedicated provision at 23:18. Retaining all of chapter 23 would hide this forecast-and-song coda after the main burden’s repeated ship-lament closure.
repairs.boss_rationale: Surface 23:15-18 as the seventy-year song and dedicated-profit coda because its temporal frame, quoted song, remembered-city outcome, and consecrated-gain reversal are complete. It remains a child of the Tyre burden, but its opening formula and changed horizon outweigh a chapter-wide flattening.

primary_reviews.support: Vehayah bayyom hahu plus the numbered period opens the coda; the song imperative and vehayah sequence conclude with qodesh profit language.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Repeated Tyre, commerce, hire, and merchandise terms continue the burden’s subject without a new named heading.

primary_reviews.support: Forgetting, minstrel song, renewed recognition, returned trade, and transformed use of gain create an ironic post-judgment afterpiece.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The coda has limited independence because the reason for forgetting and returning lies in verses 1-14.

primary_reviews.support: Separate retrieval distinguishes downfall from the later commercial reversal while mandatory parent context prevents the latter from sounding like unqualified endorsement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The seventy-year figure remains translation and chronology evidence only, not a seam beyond its explicit local formula.

repairs.defensible_basis: Behold, YHWH empties the earth opens universal leveling, covenant-breaking, curse, withered joy, silenced wine and song, shut houses, desolate city, and an olive-gleaning simile at 24:13. Flattening all of chapter 24 misses the audible turn to distant praise at verse 14, though the later midverse lament complicates finer division.
repairs.boss_rationale: End the first world-city judgment tableau at 24:13, where gleaning imagery summarizes what remains after the city’s emptied joy. Verse 14 changes to raised voices and western acclamation, providing a defensible verse-level seam; the entire 24:1-23 chapter remains an alternative if the verse-16 speaker pivot controls retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Hinneh YHWH opens the devastation; curse and covenant language drive the judgment until olive-beating and post-vintage gleaning provide a terminal remnant simile.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 14’s singing may be an internal response within the same cosmic judgment rather than a new top-level child.

primary_reviews.support: Because the decisive voice reversal occurs inside 24:16 rather than at verse 14, a whole 24:1-23 unit may better respect the poem at verse granularity.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift from emptied music to newly raised voices at 24:14 is perceptible and preserves the later complex as a larger held parent.

challenge.claim: The active 24:13 endpoint may anticipate a form break whose strongest pivot is actually intra-verse at 24:16.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain 24:1-23 as the coarse verse-granular alternative pending clause-level Hebrew and voice review.

primary_reviews.support: Chapter-scale retrieval may be safer in 24-27 because songs, laments, and cosmic judgment repeatedly interlock across short verse seams.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A 24:1-13 child has a complete desolation-to-gleaning contour and can be hydrated with the entire chapter.

challenge.claim: Finer segmentation of chapter 24 may create apparently independent fragments around a disputed speaker change.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require chapter-parent hydration and preserve whole-chapter presentation as a nonblocking competing route.

repairs.defensible_basis: Raised western voices begin at 24:14 and spread glory calls eastward, but the speaker turns inside 24:16 from songs of the righteous to personal wasting and treachery; fear-pit-snare, shattered earth, punishment of heavenly and earthly powers, and Zion’s reign then continue through 24:23. A split between verses 16 and 17 would falsely locate a clause-internal pivot at a verse edge.
repairs.boss_rationale: Hold 24:14-23 as the surfaced parent because its praise-to-lament transition cannot be represented exactly by whole-verse boundaries. The 14-16 plus 17-23 route approximates the shift, while 24:1-23 avoids approximation by staying coarser; neither option may be promoted without independent Hebrew voice and literary adjudication.

primary_reviews.support: The first-person lament begins after praise within verse 16, and the available OSHB/UXLC WLC-family evidence cannot turn that clause seam into an exact verse boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Fear, pit, and snare clearly launch a new judgment sequence at verse 17 even if the emotional pivot starts earlier.

primary_reviews.support: Praise in 14-16 and terror-to-enthronement in 17-23 are recognizable movements, but the lament’s intra-verse entrance makes a clean child split impossible in the current address model.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retaining 14-23 preserves all voices but under-exposes the real praise, lament, and cosmic judgment changes.

challenge.claim: The frozen larger unit sacrifices literary precision to verse-address precision.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Either authorize clause-level children or retain whole 24:1-23; do not pretend that 16/17 exactly captures the speaker pivot.

primary_reviews.support: A user receiving 24:14-23 alone may not see that its song responds to the emptied-earth tableau in 24:1-13.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Mandatory chapter hydration supplies that relationship while retaining the held child’s verse-exact coverage.

challenge.claim: The parent-only choice remains unresolved between 24:14-23 and the entire chapter.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Queue the two explicit presentation options for human or external-AI review after independent Hebrew discourse analysis.

repairs.defensible_basis: The first-person YHWH-my-God praise opens a thanksgiving for fulfilled counsels, a city made ruin, strong peoples giving glory, and divine refuge for poor and needy; storm, heat, cloud, and silenced-ruthless imagery resolve at 25:5. Merging the mountain feast at 25:6 would cross from retrospective hymn to a new universal banquet scene.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 25:1-5 as the city-reversal and refuge hymn because direct praise, reasons, social response, shelter metaphors, and silenced oppressors form a complete thanksgiving. The feast belongs beside it within the 24-27 parent, but its on-this-mountain opening, nations scope, and future action begin another poetic movement.

primary_reviews.support: YHWH elohay and first-person exaltation open the hymn; repeated refuge and heat imagery concludes with the song of the ruthless being subdued.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Mountain and nations vocabulary anticipate verse 6, creating a smooth thematic transition rather than a hard break.

primary_reviews.support: Praise for past counsel proceeds through ruined stronghold, honoring nations, refuge for vulnerable people, and quieted violence to closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A larger 25:1-12 hymn sequence would keep city reversal, feast, death removal, and enemy abasement together.

primary_reviews.support: The local hymn is independently coherent when hydrated with chapter 25, and it avoids letting the famous feast dominate the prior refuge movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later reuse of refuge or feast imagery can guide cross-reference but does not supply a boundary vote.

repairs.defensible_basis: On this mountain at 25:6 begins a feast for all peoples, removal of the covering, swallowing of death, wiped tears, ended reproach, and a communal acclamation that this is the awaited saving God at 25:9. Extending through 25:12 would add Moab’s trampling and demolished fortifications after the praise reaches its own joyful close.
repairs.boss_rationale: End the feast-and-death-removal poem at 25:9 because the gathered community interprets the preceding actions and concludes in rejoicing. The proposal for 25:6-12 preserves mountain continuity, but it joins a universal salvation tableau to a sharply particular abasement coda whose tone and target reset in verse 10.

primary_reviews.support: Ve’asah YHWH opens divine banquet action; swallowing, wiping, and removing are followed by vehayah bayyom hahu and a complete communal salvation acclamation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ki-tanuah at verse 10 grounds the next judgment on the same mountain and can continue the declared day.

primary_reviews.support: Feast, universal removal, rejoicing, divine hand on the mountain, and Moab’s abasement may form one 25:6-12 reversal composition.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 9 supplies an unmistakable celebratory close before addressee, image, and tone move to trampling.

challenge.claim: The frozen endpoint may separate the positive and negative outcomes of one mountain oracle.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Preserve 25:6-12 as the larger literary alternative, with 25:6-9 and 25:10-12 available only as hydrated children.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieving only 25:6-9 can foreground universal consolation while hiding the adjacent adversarial coda attached to the same mountain setting.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The full chapter parent exposes both outcomes without forcing unlike forms into one active child.

challenge.claim: The salvation child may be selectively retrieved apart from its immediate judgment contrast.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Mandate 25:1-12 hydration and retain whole 25:6-12 presentation as an append-only alternative.

repairs.defensible_basis: The divine hand resting on this mountain at 25:10 turns to Moab trampled like straw, a swimmer spreading hands but brought low, and high fortress walls cast down to dust at 25:12. Retaining 25:6-12 keeps shared setting but subordinates this targeted abasement coda to a feast-and-rejoicing poem that has already closed.
repairs.boss_rationale: Surface 25:10-12 as the Moab abasement coda because new target, degrading simile, pride reduction, and fortress demolition create a compact terminal judgment. It remains joined to 25:6-9 by mountain context, yet the distinct rhetorical action makes a separate hydrated child more exact than an undifferentiated 6-12 span.

primary_reviews.support: Ki-tanuah introduces the hand-resting rationale and named target, while three abasement verbs drive the saying to its dust-level endpoint.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The causal opening and repeated mountain setting attach the coda closely to the feast movement before it.

primary_reviews.support: The same mountain supports both feast and enemy abasement, suggesting a single positive-negative 25:6-12 oracle rather than two top-level children.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Communal rejoicing closes verse 9, after which tone, target, and dominant imagery change abruptly.

challenge.claim: Separating the coda may understate its designed contrast with the mountain feast.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Keep 25:6-12 as a parent-level alternative and require sibling hydration whenever 25:10-12 is returned.

primary_reviews.support: A named-target child avoids blending universal feast language and a particular judgment into one generalized theological proposition.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The child must never be presented without the 25:6-12 context that supplies its connective opening.

repairs.defensible_basis: The introduced song for Judah begins with a strong city and open gates, calls for perpetual trust in YHWH, contrasts the lofty city brought down, and ends with poor and needy feet trampling it at 26:6. Merging from 25:6 would cross a chapter and explicit song formula; extending to 26:7 would shift from city-trust praise to the path of the righteous and communal longing.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 26:1-6 as the strong-city trust song because its announced performance, gates, steadfast mind, everlasting rock, lowered city, and social reversal complete one lyric movement. The larger 26:1-21 option offers chapter-scale continuity, but verse 7 changes governing image, voice, and petitionary register.

primary_reviews.support: Bayyom hahu yushar hashir introduces the song, imperative gate and trust language organize it, and foot-trampling imagery supplies the final reversal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The righteous vocabulary at 26:2 continues into the righteous path at 26:7, making the seam semantically porous.

primary_reviews.support: Secure city, admitted faithful nation, steadfast trust, humbled height, and trampling by the lowly produce a balanced city-reversal hymn.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The chapter’s song and prayer may be read as one collective response across verses 1-21.

primary_reviews.support: A short 26:1-6 child may detach trust language from the waiting, judgment, and resurrection hope developed later in the chapter.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The song has an explicit start and complete city contrast; mandatory chapter hydration retains the subsequent prayer.

challenge.claim: Focused retrieval could over-isolate the strong-city hymn from its 26:1-21 communal setting.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require 26:1-21 parent hydration while retaining the exact 26:1-6 song boundary.

repairs.defensible_basis: The path of the righteous at 26:7 begins a communal address about waiting, remembered name, night desire, learning justice, and the wicked failing to perceive favor; uplifted divine hand and fire for adversaries close at 26:11. Retaining 26:7-19 would join this judgment plea to a new direct confession of peace, failed rulers, birth pangs, and awakening dead at verse 12.
repairs.boss_rationale: End the righteous-path longing and judgment plea at 26:11, where the unseen raised hand becomes zeal and consuming fire. The 26:7-19 proposal has real prayer continuity, but verse 12 begins a fresh second-person declaration of accomplished peace that develops toward an awakening climax, making 7-11 a defensible first movement.

primary_reviews.support: Path and judgment vocabulary opens at verse 7; first-person plural waiting and first-person desire proceed until the lifted-hand and fire petition closes verse 11.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Direct address to YHWH and communal voice continue into verse 12, so no new speaker enters at the seam.

primary_reviews.support: Longing for judgment in 7-11, confession in 12-15, failed-birth lament in 16-18, and awakening in 19 can form one 26:7-19 prayer movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 12’s peace declaration changes rhetorical posture after the adversary-fire ending and supports a new internal child.

challenge.claim: The frozen 7-11 child may over-split a sustained communal prayer whose climax arrives at 26:19.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain 26:7-19 as the primary larger literary alternative and test whether 7-11 plus 12-19 require compulsory sibling hydration.

primary_reviews.support: A broader 26:1-21 presentation keeps city song, communal longing, birth failure, awakening, and protective invitation within one canonical prayer sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Such breadth obscures multiple actual form changes, and parent hydration can supply context without flattening them.

challenge.claim: The active child may be too narrow for safe standalone retrieval of the communal plea.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Return 26:7-11 only with the 26:1-21 parent and preserve the coarser chapter-movement route for convergence review.
